summary:
Kars province stands under the national framework of Turkey. The sources underlying this record contain no statute, incident, court decision or enforcement record specific to Kars, so the assessment for a trans visitor to Kars rests on the country-wide pattern documented below, and nothing in the material indicates that provincial practice departs from that pattern in either direction.

Turkey's stated policy direction is toward further criminalisation. A Human Rights Watch release of 29 October 2025 reports a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal would face up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would drive treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

The draft had not been enacted when reported, but authorities have already been applying prohibitions to people as though they were in force. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped around 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police imposed no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as enforcement was being applied to them.

Document checks are the recurring point of exposure for a visitor. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, with the outing risk that implies.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender people were the most affected group. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring records roughly 313 violations against LGBTI+ people in a single year, about 2.5 times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — and systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. The government has framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma, and a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Kaos GL's 2025 review describes hostility toward LGBTI+ people having become explicit state policy: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members, and artistic events cancelled or banned. The same monitoring records 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The depth of the pattern is documented over time rather than newly established. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, recorded continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is evidence of the regime's persistence, not a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Trans prisoners in Turkey are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Branches of the Human Rights Association in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinated demands for an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 and confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison, placing custody conditions for trans prisoners under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, with online framing contested as an "LGBT opening".
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kars-specific source is present in the inventory: there is no record of a Kars statute, arrest, court decision, police practice, Pride event, healthcare facility or violent incident. Whether Kars provincial police conduct GBT-style stops, and whether facilities or care providers in Kars apply the national pattern as written, is unresolved and not sourced here.

The status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved in the material: the draft was leaked and reported in October 2025 and had not been passed at that point. Its enactment, and any change to its provisions since reporting, are not sourced.

The Kaos GL totals of 313 violations and 299 detention decisions are national figures with no provincial breakdown, so no share of them can be attributed to Kars or to north-eastern Turkey. The same applies to the 2025 Istanbul street stops, the Pride-week monitoring and the Sincan prison case, which are single-city or single-institution data points illustrating a national pattern rather than evidence about Kars.
